matching.reasoningTemplate: Colicky pain with distension and vomiting and absolute constipation suggests obstruction.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e, Chap. 16 Abdominal Pain pp.110-113; Chap. 53 Abdominal Swelling and Ascites p.327; Chap. 333 Gastrointestinal Endoscopy p.2485; GI symptom evaluation chapter (loss of bowel sounds vs hyperactive sounds)
clinicalPearls: Small-bowel obstruction characteristically produces poorly localized, intermittent peri-/supra-umbilical colicky pain; as the bowel progressively dilates and loses muscular tone the colicky quality of the pain may actually diminish, which can be falsely reassuring (p.110).

Colonic obstruction tends to cause lower-intensity colicky pain located in the infraumbilical area, often radiating to the lumbar region, in contrast to the more periumbilical pain of small-bowel obstruction (p.110).

High-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds are characteristic of mechanical obstruction, whereas loss of bowel sounds points toward ileus; however, once proximal bowel becomes markedly distended and edematous, peristaltic sounds may become weak or absent even without peritonitis.

Auscultation is one of the least revealing parts of the abdominal exam: a strangulating small-intestinal obstruction can occur with normal-sounding peristalsis, so normal bowel sounds do not exclude a catastrophe (p.113).

Patients with obstructive colic tend to be restless and may thrash about, in contrast to the peritonitic patient who lies still to avoid movement — a useful bedside discriminator when ischaemia/perforation supervenes (p.110).

Inability to pass stool or flatus combined with nausea/vomiting and increasing abdominal girth suggests bowel obstruction (or severe constipation/ileus); retained feces in the colon itself adds to the distension (p.327).
harrison.pathophysiology: Mechanical obstruction of a hollow viscus classically elicits intermittent (colicky) pain that is less well localized than the parietal pain of peritoneal irritation; distension of the viscus may also produce steady pain with only occasional paroxysms. With superimposed strangulating obstruction, traction on the root of the mesentery can refer pain to the lower lumbar region. As the obstructed proximal bowel progressively dilates it loses muscular tone, so colicky pain may wane and peristaltic sounds may weaken. Obstruction must be distinguished from adynamic ileus (loss of peristalsis) and from colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome), in which the bowel is dilated without a mechanical lesion (Harrison 22e pp.110-113, p.327).
additionalDifferentials: Adynamic / paralytic ileus (loss of peristalsis with absent bowel sounds) rather than mechanical obstruction
Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) — colonic dilatation without a mechanical lesion
Severe constipation / fecal impaction causing abdominal distension and discomfort
Sigmoid or cecal volvulus as a cause of colonic obstruction
Gastric outlet obstruction (malignancy or chronic peptic stenosis of the pylorus) presenting with vomiting of partially digested food hours after eating
Esophageal obstruction by impacted food bolus / foreign body (proximal obstruction mimic)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute mesenteric arterial occlusion — early diffuse cramping pain from hyperperistalsis with 'pain out of proportion to physical findings' can mimic early obstruction; tenderness and rigidity may be absent until vascular collapse
Porphyria and lead colic — severe hyperperistalsis makes the pain difficult to distinguish from intestinal obstruction
Diabetic ketoacidosis — can both precipitate and mimic an acute abdomen; if pain does not resolve with metabolic correction, suspect an organic cause such as obstruction
Irritable bowel syndrome — functional pain with altered bowel habit, but nausea/vomiting are rare and localized tenderness/spasm inconsistent (a non-obstructive mimic of altered bowel habit)
additionalInvestigations: Low-dose CT is preferred over plain abdominal radiography when the indication for surgical/medical intervention is unclear in nontraumatic acute abdominal pain

Plain upright/lateral-decubitus abdominal radiographs can show dilated bowel loops suggesting obstruction or ileus, but have limited utility and may be unnecessary when the cause (e.g., strangulated external hernia) is already evident
Water-soluble contrast enema can be diagnostic in suspected colonic obstruction without perforation; oral barium sulfate should be avoided if colonic obstruction is suspected
Serum amylase may be raised by strangulating intestinal obstruction (also by perforated ulcer, cholecystitis), so an elevation neither confirms nor excludes the need for operation

Leukocytosis is non-specific (a WBC >20,000/uL may follow perforation but also pancreatitis, cholecystitis, infarction) and should never be the sole determinant of operative need; a normal count does not exclude perforation

Endoscopy can diagnose and often manage gastroduodenal and colonic obstruction/pseudo-obstruction, but small-bowel obstruction from surgical adhesions is generally neither diagnosed nor treated endoscopically
redFlags: Continuous diffuse pain with absent tenderness/rigidity ('pain out of proportion to findings') in a patient at vascular risk — suspect superior mesenteric artery occlusion / intestinal ischaemia
Spread of pain to the lower lumbar region — may indicate strangulating obstruction with traction on the mesenteric root
Truly silent abdomen with sudden severe pain — suggests chemical peritonitis from a perforated viscus

Catastrophic intra-abdominal events may present with minimal or no pain/muscle spasm in obtunded, debilitated, immunosuppressed, or elderly patients — a slowly developing process also attenuates guarding
pitfalls: Relying on auscultation or bowel-sound quality: strangulating obstruction can occur with normal peristaltic sounds, and distended/edematous proximal bowel may be quiet even without peritonitis (p.113).
Interpreting waning colicky pain as improvement — pain may diminish simply because the dilated bowel has lost muscular tone (p.110).
Using leukocytosis or serum amylase as a deciding factor for surgery — both are non-specific in obstruction and infarction (p.113).
Giving oral barium when colonic obstruction is possible (risk of inspissation above the obstruction); use water-soluble contrast instead.
Missing intestinal ischaemia, which classically elicits severe pain but little tenderness (GI evaluation chapter).
